images.title: Bridges through time
images.caption: View over Vltava River, Prague, Czechia
images.desc: This autumnal view from Letná Park looks out over Prague, which grew up along the banks of the Vltava River in Czechia. In today's image, the river winds its way through the historic Old Town and Malá Strana districts, beneath Mánes Bridge in the foreground. Many beautiful bridges now span the Vltava, but for centuries there was only one, Charles Bridge, pictured second from the bottom. Its first stones were laid in 1357 during the reign of Charles IV and until 1841, it was the only way to cross the river on foot. Today its stone arches, gothic towers, and statues lining the bridge draw large crowds, so tourists are advised to get there by dawn for the best photographs. Or they could walk on to the next crossing, Legion Bridge, which is less crowded and offers beautiful views of the National Theatre, Prague Castle, and its busier neighbor.

images.title: Ribbons of gray and gold
images.caption: Face Canyon, Lake Powell, Utah
images.desc: Hidden within an ancient sandstone landscape, Face Canyon is one of 96 canyons stretching out from Lake Powell in southern Utah. Many are far from roads and would be hard to reach if they hadn't been flooded by the lake, created in 1963 during the construction of the Glen Canyon Dam. The lake's waters back up about 186 miles, along creeks and canyons which you can explore by boat, kayak, or personal watercraft.

images.copyright: Two wild tom turkeys (© davidsdodd/Getty Images)
images.title: Turkey twins
images.caption: Happy Thanksgiving!
images.desc: With their colorful plumage and distinctive gobble, adult male turkeys, known as toms or gobblers, are a familiar sight of the season. Toms, like those pictured here, fan their tail feathers and show off their rich coloring to attract hens. These native birds can be found in the wild across much of North America, often in forest and woodland habitats. Turkeys have also become closely tied to Thanksgiving traditions, serving as a familiar centerpiece of a holiday feast that, for many, is less about what's on the table and more about gathering with family and friends. In today's image, two toms take a Thanksgiving stroll and put their finest feathers forward in the warm glow of autumn.

images.title: A southwestern snowfall
images.caption: Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah
images.desc: Snow transforms Bryce Canyon National Park, blanketing the landscape in white while its fiery orange-red hoodoos rise above the snowy terrain. Seen from Sunset Point, one of the park's most famous overlooks, these fantastical shapes are part of the Claron Formation, whose limestone was deposited about 50 million years ago and later shaped by weathering and erosion. Because much of the park rises above 8,000 feet, snow can arrive as early as October. In today's image, snow clings to the canyon's ridges and spires while mist drifts across the cliffs, creating an iconic winter scene in the American Southwest.

images.title: Autumnal camouflage
images.caption: Red squirrel in Cairngorms National Park, Scotland
images.desc: As Britain's only native squirrel species, red squirrels thrive in Scotland's Cairngorms National Park. An important refuge, the park offers ancient Caledonian pine forests and newer conifer woodlands, with plentiful habitat and food for squirrels foraging for Scots pine seeds, nuts, and other tasty morsels year-round. In today's image, a red squirrel is perched amid warm orange and yellow leaves, looking right at home as it ponders its next move in the Scottish Highlands.

images.title: Geometry in nature
images.caption: Fibonacci Day
images.desc: Today's image shows the gradual coiling of a young fiddlehead's tip, echoing the geometric patterns seen throughout nature. In math, the Fibonacci sequence follows a similar progression, each number formed by adding the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and so on. Today is Fibonacci Day, chosen for the numbers of the date (11/23) to honor the sequence. Eventually the young fern frond shown here will unfurl as it grows, but elsewhere in the plant world, the sequence will continue to appear in the spiraling arrangements of sunflower heads, pinecones, succulents, and pineapples.

images.title: Shelter among the waves
images.caption: The chapel and hermitage of Santa Justa in Cantabria, Spain
images.desc: Tucked into the cliffs of northern Spain's rugged coastline, the 16th-century Hermitage of Santa Justa seen in today's image overlooks the crashing waves of the Cantabrian Sea. Built partly into the rock and associated with relics of Saints Justa and Rufina, the small chapel eventually became a pilgrimage site, its sheltered stone walls creating a remarkable contrast with the powerful waves and rocky cliffs surrounding it.

images.title: Terracotta dreams
images.caption: Nice, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France
images.desc: Bathed in a sun-kissed glow, Nice is a patchwork of terracotta rooftops, historic churches, and pastel façades along the French Riviera, as seen in today's image. Founded by ancient Greeks and long connected to the Italian royal House of Savoy, Nice officially became part of France in 1860. Today, that layered past remains visible throughout the coastal city in the south of France, where old-world architecture meets the blue Mediterranean waters and sunlit hills of the Côte d'Azur.
